rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field experiment (2005-2007) at Citra FL with factorial irrigation x N-rate treatments and own measurements. Q2: Table 1 reports irrigation applied of 78/186/227 mm for capacitance-sensor (ECH2O/QIC) SUR vs 215/391/380 mm for TIME; Fig 3 and Section 3.2 show percolated volume reduced; Table 5/Fig 4 show NO3-N leaching cut by ~90% under SMS treatments; abstract states SMS-based systems significantly reduced irrigation water use, percolation and nitrate leaching. Q3: Abstract and Section 3.2 state leaching reduction was detected both by drainage lysimeters (Table 5, Fig 4) and independently by Hydra Probe soil moisture/EC monitoring at 0.12, 0.37 and 0.67 m (Fig 6), which showed no moisture or EC spikes at depth under SMS treatments. Q4: Fig 6 and Section 3.2 measure soil water content dynamics: TIME produced moisture spikes above 0.20 m3 m-3 (above field capacity) that drained to 0.37 and 0.67 m, whereas SMS treatments kept moisture relatively constant; authors describe this as the mechanistic driving force for the leaching difference. Q8: Section 2 notes the twin irrigation/fertigation line setup was for experimental convenience and a commercial grower would likely use a single surface line; Section 3.2 notes EC measurements were not ion-specific so other ions may have influenced readings. Q9: Fig 3 (cumulative leachate volume) and Fig 4 (nitrate leaching) report error bars as standard error of the mean (n=4).
rows.notes: Water savings themselves (Table 1 irrigation volumes) are drawn from the same experiment and detailed in the companion paper Zotarelli et al. 2009; this paper still tabulates them and reports percolation and leaching. Q3 'yes' rests on lysimeters plus capacitance probe moisture/EC monitoring for reduced deep percolation/leaching; irrigation volume itself was measured by one method. Q7: statements that high-frequency low-volume irrigation suits sandy soils are interpretive scope statements, not stated requirements, so rated no. Single site, single sandy soil, single crop over three years.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field experiment at Citra FL with own biomass, N and leaching measurements. Q2: Table 3 and Section 3.1 report fruit dry biomass 37%, 17% and 16% higher for sensor-based SUR/SDI than TIME in 2005, 2006, 2007, and shoot dry weight and total N accumulation significantly higher (Table 2, P<=0.01); text states SMS control generally increased shoot and fruit dry weight. Q4: Section 3.1, Table 4 and Fig 2 measure the intermediate pathway: petiole sap NO3 and leaf N higher under SMS, N-uptake rates and above-ground N accumulation higher, and authors link excessive leaching under TIME to reduced N uptake, hampered canopy development and yield; Fig 6 shows soil moisture dynamics. Q8: Section 2 states the twin drip line setup was for experimental convenience and differs from commercial practice; biomass sampling based on one representative plant per plot (Section 2.1). Q9: Table 2 reports CV% for shoot and fruit dry biomass; Fig 2 shows standard error bars (n=4) for N accumulation.
rows.notes: Fresh marketable yield results (11-26% increase for SDI/SUR) are only cited from the companion paper Zotarelli et al. 2009; this paper's own crop-production evidence is fruit and shoot dry biomass and N accumulation. Yield measured by a single method (destructive harvest), so no triangulation. No support conditions stated as requirements. Single site, soil and crop.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study uses capacitance sensors (ECH2O probe with QIC controller) to trigger irrigation under plastic mulch drip on tomato; companion paper (Zotarelli et al. 2009, AWM 96:23-34) holds the irrigation water use efficiency and marketable yield results from the same trial.
